Fixed in 6c3e261. ~F no longer widens the f32 to f64 (1.0e-10 printed 0.0000000001000000013351432), keeps the trailing point including at ~,0F ('4.' not '4'), and ~E now uses a lowercase marker with a signed exponent (1.0e+10). Key finding: ~F uses TWO rounding regimes - pad with zeros when more fraction digits are requested than the shortest decimal carries (so ~,3F of 3.4028235e38 is ...350000...000, not the exact binary value), and round the EXACT value with ties away from zero when fewer are requested (~,2F of 1.005 is 1.00 since that f32 is 1.00499999523162841796875; ~,1F of 0.25 is 0.3 since that f32 is exact). Rust's {:.N} rounds half-to-even and gets 0.25 wrong, so rounding is done on the digit string. Fixed in 67efc9b. Root cause was NOT the rooted-list machinery (four hypotheses there all disproven by instrumentation) but a heap-exhaustion corruption chain: CLOS instances were allocated in the nursery then pinned, each pinned nursery object forced its whole 1MB region to be retained forever (~316 instances poisoned 316 of 512 regions, census-verified), nothing could reclaim anything (old_occupancy_trigger was dead config, no automatic major GC, Survivor regions unreclaimable by ANY collector), and when 0 Free regions remained, minor evacuation SILENTLY DROPPED live objects - roots kept stale pointers, the nursery was zeroed under them, and the mutator read a corrupted macro-expansion form as 'unbound variable: CONS'.

Fixes: instances allocate directly into packed pinned-host regions (no nursery retention); pinned allocs pack into dedicated hosts that ordinary evacuation never targets; old_occupancy_trigger wired to run a major after a crossing minor; major treats Survivor like OldGen (evacuate <50% live, free zero-live); size-aware target-region finder (the fixed '>header+align' test could lose objects even with Free regions available); evacuation failure is now a loud panic with a region census, and the major frees only fully-evacuated regions ('let _ = copy_object' used to swallow failure then free the region, zeroing live objects).

THE CLAIM: "a loop whose body calls builtins is never promoted; it runs T0
while an empty loop reaches 0.012 us/iter", evidenced by direct=9 fallback=845
through the native adapters on an 8M-iteration loop.

WHY IT WAS WRONG: that measurement was taken while direct_builtin_slot was
still rejecting EVERY builtin (the shadow check tested whether a function cell
existed, but builtins carry one so #'aref works; the right test is whether it
is an INTERPRETED function). With the resolver refusing everything, the emitter
never chose the builtin adapter, so neither of its counters could fire. I read
"the adapter was never emitted" as "the loop never went native". Those are very
different things and I did not distinguish them.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, measured three ways:

 1. bliss-ext:function-osr-count reports 1 OSR entry for EACH of empty-loop,
    add-loop and aref-loop. The aref loop promotes.
 2. compile_osr_code emits through emit_native_x86 -- the SAME emitter the
    direct-builtin work wired -- so OSR'd code gets direct builtin calls too.
 3. With the counters split into native versus interpreter, the same
    8M-iteration loop reports:

        native:      direct=40,500,007  fallback=890
        interpreter: direct=   500,080  fallback=187

    40.5M of the ~41M builtin calls happen in NATIVE code taking the direct
    path. The 500k interpreted ones are the pre-OSR warmup.

So there is no "loops with builtin calls never promote" bug. The empty loop's
0.012 us/iter versus the aref loop's 0.170 is simply the cost of three builtin
calls per iteration in native code, not a tiering failure.

WHERE THE REMAINING COST ACTUALLY IS, and it is bliss-edzd: ~0.157 us/iter over
three calls is ~0.052 us per direct builtin call. That call no longer does any
symbol->name->symbol resolution, but call_direct_builtin still reaches the
kernels through apply_numeric_op / apply_builtin_fast / apply_builtin, which
match on `name: &str`. Dispatching on the TABLE SLOT instead of the name is the
remaining half of bliss-edzd, and the table added in 8fbcc66 is the natural
place to hang it.

Lesson for the next person: a counter that only increments on a path the
compiler chose cannot distinguish "path not taken" from "path not emitted".
Count both sides, and separate native from interpreted.

ROOT CAUSE, and a correction to an earlier comment of mine on this bead: this is test interference over a single global coordinator, NOT a race the production runtime can reach. I had argued the three failure modes meant unsynchronised registry access and that isolating the tests would HIDE a real race. Reading the tests disproves that:

 - lazily_registered_host_threads_... samples a GLOBAL participant count before/during/after, and make_thread_join_... bounds all_thread_ids().len(); any other test spawning or joining a thread moves those numbers.
 - stop_the_world_... and t0_alloc_typed_... call wait_for_all_threads()/resume_all_threads() and then assert their thread stayed parked; a concurrent test's resume_all_threads() restarts it.
 - Decisively, failed_safepoint_handshake_is_reported_and_cleans_up DELIBERATELY creates a thread that never polls, so while it runs every other rendezvous in the process is MEANT to fail.
 - test_safepoint.rs had no serialization at all, and its tests contradict each other over the one mprotected safepoint page (safepoint_initially_not_requested vs a concurrent request_then_resume_cycle).

One cause, three symptoms: wrong counts, wrong stop-the-world assertions, and hangs/faults when two rendezvous overlap and each waits on threads the other resumed. There is one collector and nothing outside a test harness drives two simultaneous handshakes, so the original bead title was right and my reframing was not.

The bead's open question -- libc setenv is not async-signal-safe and mutates a
process-global environ, so do we need our own lock or our own environment block?
-- resolves to NEITHER. std's unix env shim holds an RwLock across getenv /
setenv / unsetenv, so TorCL's own GETENV (std::env::var) and SETENV are already
serialized against each other no matter how many threads race; and a private
environment block would diverge from what a child process inherits and what FFI
code reads, which is the whole point of being able to set a variable. The
residual hazard the edition-2024 `unsafe` marks is non-Rust code calling libc
getenv, which does not take that lock; the SAFETY comment says so.
